the-challenge-of-natural-hazards: In one Aceh village, the 2004 tsunami killed four females for every male. Why would a wave "choose"?
The Atlantic is about 2.5 cm wider every year. What moves the plates?
Nepal 2015 and Kaikōura 2016 were both magnitude 7.8. One killed more than 8,790 people; the other killed 2. Why?
About 800 million people live near active volcanoes. Why don't they move away?
Why are the world's rainforests and hottest deserts found in bands either side of the equator?
Hurricane Ian hit Florida with 130-knot winds in 2022. Why was water, not wind, its deadliest hazard?
A hurricane hit Cuba, then Florida. The USA is far richer than Cuba, so why did far more people die in Florida?
A Cornish village once got three times July's average rain in three hours. Why did it flood so fast?
the-living-world: What happens to a whole pond when just one thing in it changes?
Rainforest at the equator, desert a little further north. Why do the world's big ecosystems come in bands?
Rainforest soils are surprisingly poor. So how do they grow such huge, rich forests?
The world's biggest rainforest is still being cleared. Who is doing it, and why does it matter beyond Brazil?
Some villagers in Guatemala make a living by cutting down rainforest trees. Can logging help save a forest?
Antarctica is covered in ice, yet it counts as a desert. How?
Many people in the Australian opal town of Coober Pedy live in homes dug into rock. Why live underground?
Between 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, the Sahara had permanent lakes, plants and people. Today it is desert. Did people cause the change?
Winter brings little or no sunlight, and winds can gust at well over 200 km/h. How does anything live there?
About half of the 800-mile Trans-Alaska Pipeline runs above the ground. Why not bury all of it?
Over 100,000 tourists a year now visit Antarctica. Who decides how to keep it wild?
physical-landscapes-in-the-uk: Why are most of Britain's mountains in the north and west, and its flattest land in the south and east?
Between 1951 and 2004 the cliffs at Aldbrough, on England's Holderness coast, retreated about 2 m a year. Why do they disappear so fast?
Spurn Point is over three miles long and in places only 50 m wide. How did a finger of sand form across the mouth of the Humber?
Over 1,000 years, one English coast has lost 26 villages to the sea. Where did all that land go?
By 2014 the Environment Agency had built new banks inland at Medmerry, West Sussex, and let the sea flood the land between. Why give land to the sea?
A silt grain is one-hundredth the width of a coarse sand grain, yet water must flow about three times as fast to pick it up. Why?
Niagara Falls has moved about 7 miles (11 km) upstream in about 12,000 years. How does a waterfall move backwards?
Why does the River Tees plunge over a cliff in the Pennines but loop lazily near the sea?

On 23 December 2013, 43–45 mm of rain fell on two river basins in southern England. Within a day, one river surged to one of its highest flows since records began; the other barely rose, and peaked only in mid-February after weeks more rain. Why did the same storm have such different effects?
In 1995, more than 250,000 people in the Netherlands had to leave their homes as the rivers rose. The Dutch response was not simply higher dikes. What did they do?
Why did Leeds build river gates that fall flat just when a flood arrives?
urban-issues-challenges: In 1979 Shenzhen was what its government calls "a small backward border town". By 2024 it had 17.98 million residents. Where did they all come from?
Mumbai keeps drawing people in from across India. Who really gains from its growth?
In 2011, 1 in 10 people in Mumbai's D ward lived in slums. In M/East ward, more than 3 in 4 did. Why such a gap inside one city?
London is more than 600 times as crowded as the Highlands. Why do people cluster where they do?
London produces more per person than any other UK region. So why can so many Londoners not afford a home?
London builds most of its new homes on old, used land. Why not just build on the fields around it?
Two neighbourhoods on two continents: both were demolished and redeveloped. Who decides what replaces a neighbourhood?
Urban areas use 75% of the world's energy. Vauban, a whole eco-district in Germany, is home to about 5,300 people. Can eco-cities and smart cities make a real difference?
In 2003 London began charging drivers to enter its centre. By 2007 traffic was still lower, but congestion was back where it started. How?
the-changing-economic-world: Guyana's income per person is more than three and a half times Sri Lanka's. Why do they have exactly the same HDI?
At today's rate, Niger's population would double in about 21 years. Japan's is shrinking. Why?
Why does a baby born in Norway expect to live about 25 years longer than one born in Somalia?
In 2022 Sri Lanka defaulted on its foreign debt and turned to the IMF. Who sets the terms of rescue loans, and is there an alternative?
In 2006 a bank for poor villagers won the Nobel Peace Prize. Do small loans and fairer prices really lift people out of poverty?
In 2017 Rwanda doubled the price of a permit to see mountain gorillas, to US$1,500. Can making tourism more expensive make it more sustainable?
India now has more people than any other country. Why is it still only a lower-middle-income country?

Apple employs about 166,000 people. Toyota and its affiliates run more than 50 manufacturing operations in 27 countries and regions outside Japan. Why do these two giants make their products in such different ways?
India sits in clubs with both the USA and Russia. How do its friendships shape its development?
Income per person in India has risen about seven times since 1995. Who has gained, and at what cost?
the-challenge-of-resource-management: In March, April and May 2026, oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz averaged about 2.7 million barrels a day, down from about 20 million. Why did farmers and food importers far from the Gulf feel the shock?
Britain has plenty of farmland, so why does about two-fifths of its food come from abroad?
Most of Britain's rain falls in the north and west. Why is the south-east the part running short of water?
Coal once supplied most of Britain's energy. Today it supplies almost none. What took its place?
In 2023 the world's food supply came to about 3,000 calories per person per day. So why did around 645 million people go hungry in 2025?
Brazil left the UN's Hunger Map in 2014, fell back onto it, then left again in 2025. What does it take to end hunger, and to keep it ended?
Pakistan relies on the world's largest connected irrigation system. Why is salt now spoiling its fields?
In 1993 one Brazilian city declared that food is a right. What did it do to make that real?
physical-landscapes-in-the-uk-part-2: Between 1941 and 2004, Alaska's Muir Glacier retreated 12 km. All that time, its ice kept flowing towards the sea. How can both be true?
A 16,500-tonne boulder sits on the flat prairie of Alberta, Canada, far from the mountains it came from. How did it get there?
Why does the land around Helvellyn look as if a giant scooped it out with a spoon?
Walkers, sheep farmers, quarries and boats all want the same fells. Who gets to use the Lake District?
Over 17 million tourists visited the Lake District in 2025. What do all those visitors do to it?
the-challenge-of-natural-hazards-part-2: How do scientists know what Earth's climate was like 800,000 years ago, long before thermometers?
In 1991 one volcano in the Philippines cooled the whole planet. How?
The UK's emissions fell by 54% between 1990 and 2025. Has the UK really halved its part in climate change?
Global sea level has risen about 10 cm since 1993, and the yearly rise has more than doubled. Where is the extra water coming from?

In May 2024 a company opened what it called the world's largest plant for pulling CO₂ out of the air, in Iceland, designed to capture up to 36,000 tonnes a year. Could machines like it clean up our emissions?
About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level. Tuvalu's land averages about 2 m above it. Which is more vulnerable, and why?
the-challenge-of-resource-management-par: In January 2018 Cape Town, a city of just over 4 million people, warned that its taps could be turned off in April: "Day Zero". What pushed it to the edge, and how did it pull back?

The Lower Mekong's fisheries land an estimated 2.3 million tonnes of fish a year, worth about US$11 billion. Its hydropower capacity could more than double. Can one river be both a great fishery and a giant power station?
Beijing has about a twentieth of China's average water per person. Is moving a river the answer?
In dry parts of Kenya, villagers store water inside river sand. Why would sand beat an open pond?
In 2025, solar power generation grew by about 30%. In the same year, the world used more fossil fuel than ever. How can both be true?
If wind is free and never runs out, why don't we get all our electricity from it?
Northern England sits on a vast store of shale gas. Why did England stop fracking for it?
A remote Andean village got electricity from its own stream. Why did people who had left move back?
the-changing-economic-world-part-2: Detroit had 1,849,568 people in 1950 and 639,111 in 2020. What emptied the Motor City?
In 1978 a quarter of UK jobs were in manufacturing. Today it is about one in fifteen. What replaced them?
Why are some UK villages growing fast while others are losing people?
A baby boy in Hart, Hampshire can expect to live ten years longer than one in Blackpool. Why?
The UK left the European Union in 2020. So why does it still sell the EU more than anywhere else?
